glp1-body-map.title: Three places where semaglutide acts

brain.label: Brain: less hunger
brain.detail: In a trial in 72 adults, people on semaglutide took in 35% fewer calories than people on placebo at a lunch where they could eat freely. Which brain areas take part is known only from animal studies.

stomach.label: Stomach: may empty a little more slowly
stomach.detail: The label describes a small delay soon after a meal. With longer use the effect seems to fade: a 20-week trial of the weight-loss dose found no clear delay.

pancreas.label: Pancreas: more insulin when blood sugar is high
pancreas.detail: The pancreas releases more insulin and less glucagon, mainly when blood sugar is high. So on its own, semaglutide has a low risk of making blood sugar too low.

glp1-body-map.text: The picture shows the front of a head and trunk, with three organs in colour; the pancreas lies mostly behind the stomach. Number 1 is the brain: semaglutide makes people less hungry. In a trial in 72 adults with obesity, after 20 weeks people on semaglutide took in 35% fewer calories at a free-choice lunch than people on placebo. The brain areas involved are known from studies in rodents. Number 2 is the stomach: soon after a meal, it may empty a little more slowly. With longer use this effect seems to fade; in the same 20-week trial no clear delay was found. Number 3 is the pancreas: it releases more insulin and less glucagon, mainly when blood sugar is high. That is why semaglutide on its own has a low risk of low blood sugar, but the risk is not zero.

online-vial-risks.title: What may be wrong with a vial that did not come from a pharmacy

identity.label: May not be what the label says
identity.detail: The FDA warns that one name can cover different salt forms, or even a different active substance. A French lab found that products sold as TB-500 did not always match their description.

amount.label: The amount may differ from the label
amount.detail: A 2026 study in Australia tested 3 products sold as retatrutide. They held from about half to almost twice the amount on the label. The TB-500 certificates the FDA saw did not check the amount.

impurities.label: May hold near-copies and leftover chemicals
impurities.detail: Making a peptide can leave chains that are too short or slightly wrong, plus leftover solvents and other chemicals. Most certificates the FDA saw gave the purity but did not say which impurities were there.

endotoxin.label: May not be tested for bacterial toxins (endotoxin)
endotoxin.detail: For anything injected, the FDA says this test is key. The certificates it saw for BPC-157 and TB-500 did not have it.

germs.label: May not be tested for germs
germs.detail: For injections, the FDA says germ tests are key too. The certificates it saw for BPC-157, KPV and TB-500 showed no germ tests.

clumps.label: Clumps may make immune reactions more likely
clumps.detail: Peptides can stick together into clumps. The FDA says clumps and impurities may raise the risk of an immune reaction, from harmless to life-threatening. No study has tested this for BPC-157, KPV or TB-500.

online-vial-risks.text: The picture shows one small glass vial with a grey rubber stopper and some white powder at the bottom. It has no label. Six numbers show what may be wrong with a vial like this when it did not come from a pharmacy. Number 1, on the glass where a label would be: it may not be what the label says. The FDA warns that one name can cover different salt forms, or even a different active substance. A French lab found that products sold as TB-500 did not always match their description. Number 2, on the powder: the amount may differ from the label. A 2026 study in Australia tested 3 products sold as retatrutide. They held from about half to almost twice the amount on the label. The TB-500 certificates the FDA saw did not check the amount. Number 3, on the powder: making a peptide can leave chains that are too short or slightly wrong, plus leftover solvents and other chemicals. Most certificates the FDA saw gave the purity but did not say which impurities were there. Number 4, inside the vial: it may not have been tested for bacterial toxins, called endotoxin. For anything injected, the FDA says this test is key, and the certificates it saw for BPC-157 and TB-500 did not have it. Number 5, inside the vial: it may not have been tested for germs. For injections the FDA says germ tests are key too, and the certificates it saw for BPC-157, KPV and TB-500 showed no germ tests. Number 6, on the powder: peptides can stick together into clumps. The FDA says clumps and impurities may raise the risk of an immune reaction, from harmless to life-threatening. No study has tested this for BPC-157, KPV or TB-500. That is why number 6 has a different colour: it is a possible risk, not a proven one.
